y-m-18-03.title: Haeun band-graph solution: wetin look strange?

y-m-18-03.goal: For one percentage-calculation solution, find wrong line and clue say ‘if total no be 100%, e wrong,’ then make survey numbers wey give same band graph.
y-m-18-03.material: Haeun, one 6th grader, ask all 40 classmates choose one ‘favorite season.’ Results na spring 12 students, summer 14, fall 8, winter 6. Haeun solve am below to show in band graph. Whole band of band graph na 100%.
y-m-18-03.thinking.1: Checking by yourself using condition say whole na 100%

y-m-18-03.s.s2.hint.1: Change total number of people and check whether number for each choice come out as natural number of students.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.hint.2: Check whether people numbers wey you make match total students and whether percentages remain the same.

y-m-18-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Total student number must be natural number wey no pass 60.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Number of people for each choice na natural number from 0 upward.
y-m-18-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Number of people for each choice must be natural number from 0 upward.

y-m-18-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Total number of people for choices no equal total students.

y-m-18-03.s.s2.explain: If N=10, results na 4, 3, 2, 1 students, and if N=20, na 8, 6, 4, 2 students. Both times, percentages for band graph same. You fit show 40%, 30%, 20%, and 10% as natural number of people when N na multiple of 10.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.prompt: So Haeun no go make same mistake again, tell her one way she fit check by herself wetin wrong before drawing band graph.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.hint.0: Think wetin percentage whole band graph suppose be, and how you fit compare calculated values with am.
y-m-18-03.s.s3.hint.1: Read last line of Haeun solution and think wetin she suppose notice there.

y-m-18-05.title: If we join two classes, wetin be overall average?
y-m-18-05.topic: Understanding average when you combine several groups
y-m-18-05.goal: Know say averages for two groups alone no determine overall average, explain what else we need, and make student numbers by yourself wey meet conditions.
y-m-18-05.material: Class 1 and Class 2 for 6th grade do same math test. All scores from 0 to 100 points. Class 1 average na 70 points and Class 2 average na 80. Hajun talk, “Average for both classes together na (70+80)÷2=75 points.” Dem never tell how many students dey for each class.
y-m-18-05.thinking.1: Reasoning how group size move average toward one side
y-m-18-05.thinking.2: Making different combinations of people numbers wey meet conditions
y-m-18-05.prereq.1: Multiplication and addition of natural numbers
y-m-18-05.s.s1.prompt: For Hajun 75 points to be exactly correct, which thing must be known?
y-m-18-05.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine whether overall average go near 75 if Class 1 get 1 student and Class 2 get 99.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, test one by one which direction overall average go move if na true.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.o.a: Class 1 get more students than Class 2.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.a: Overall average dey move closer to average of group wey get more students. Then think whether e go be 75.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.o.b: Both classes get same number of students.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.b: This consider say group size affect average. If sizes equal, both averages count equally.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.o.c: Both classes get one student wey score 100 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.c: Even if highest score same, overall average no become middle of two averages.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.r.d: Even if all scores for Class 2 same, if class sizes differ, overall average go differ.
y-m-18-05.s.s1.explain: Only when both classes get same student number, overall average na 75 points, exactly middle of both averages. If student numbers differ, overall average move toward class wey get more students.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.prompt: Now you know Class 1 get 20 students and Class 2 get 30. How overall average compare with 75 points?
y-m-18-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think which class, the one with 20 students or 30 students, get more influence on whole through their scores.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.hint.1: Draw number line and show whether overall average between 70 and 80 go closer to one.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.a: You mix averages of two classes wey get different student numbers in equal parts.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.b: Class wey get more students na di one with higher scores, but you think say overall average go down.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.o.c: You no fit tell whether e higher or lower than 75 points.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.c: You know both class sizes and averages, so you fit fix di direction.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.r.d: You judge say overall average move toward Class 2 average of 80, because e get more students.
y-m-18-05.s.s2.explain: Class 2 get more students and higher average, so overall average above 75 points. Actually, (70×20+80×30)÷50=76 points. 2
y-m-18-05.s.s3.prompt: Class 1 average of 70 and Class 2 average of 80 stay as dem be. Make 2 different versions of student numbers so combined overall average exactly 78 points. (Class 1 get m students, Class 2 get n students; each class get at least 5, and both classes together get no more than 50.)
y-m-18-05.s.s3.hint.0: If overall average na 78 points, think whether e closer to Class 1 average 70 or Class 2 average 80.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare distance from 78 to 70 and from 78 to 80. 70 80
y-m-18-05.s.s3.hint.2: With student numbers you choose, check by yourself say overall average really na 78.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.ok.c1: Each class get natural number of 5 or more students.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Each class student number must be natural number of 5 or more.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.ok.c2: Both classes together get 50 or less.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.fail.c2: Both classes together get more than 50.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.explain: For example, with 5 students in Class 1 and 20 in Class 2, total score na 70×5+80×20=1950, divide by 25 students give 78 points. When Class 2 get 4 times as many students as Class 1, overall average na 78.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.prompt: Write why, when Class 1 get 5 students and Class 2 get 20, overall average na 78 and no be 75.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.hint.0: Compare which class score, 75 or 78 points, closer to.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.hint.1: First write how student number for both classes differ, then give reason.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: You write say class with more students get bigger effect on overall average?
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Direction say average higher than 75 and your reason agree?
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.model.0: Class 2 get 4 times as many students as Class 1, so average come closer to Class 2 score of 80. Na why e be 78, no be 75.
y-m-18-05.s.s3.because.model.1: Na because score from class with more students get bigger effect on overall average. Class 2 get 4 times as many, so overall average dey pulled toward 80.

y-m-18-06.title: Make spinner wey no favor anybody
y-m-18-06.topic: Showing chance with numbers: fair spinner
y-m-18-06.goal: Judge equal chances by number of sections, design different spinners wey meet conditions, and explain say ‘fairness’ and ‘how often somebody win’ different things.
y-m-18-06.material: Haeun and Doyun dey play spinner game. Spinner divide evenly into 12 same-size sections, and arrow get same chance to stop at any section. Each section get ‘Haeun,’ ‘Doyun,’ or ‘blank’ written inside. Person name on section where arrow stop get 1 point; if blank, nobody get point. ‘Fair’ mean both people get same chance to earn point.
y-m-18-06.thinking.0: Comparing equal chances by number of sections
y-m-18-06.thinking.2: Separating fairness from another property (how often somebody wins)
y-m-18-06.prereq.0: Meaning and comparing size of fractions 1/2, 1/4, 1/3
y-m-18-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all fair spinners from these. (All get 12 sections.)
y-m-18-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each spinner, write side by side Haeun and Doyun chances to get point as number of sections out of 12.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.hint.1: Ignore blank sections and compare only number of sections for both people.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.a: Haeun 6 sections, Doyun 3 sections, blank 3 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.a: One person get twice di number of sections of the other. Check how section number determine chance size.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.b: Haeun 5 sections, Doyun 5 sections, blank 2 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.b: You judge fairness by comparing both people section numbers, no be blank sections.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.c: Haeun 5 sections, Doyun 4 sections, blank 3 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.c: 5 sections and 4 sections look close, but chances no be same.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.o.d: Haeun 4 sections, Doyun 4 sections, blank 4 sections
y-m-18-06.s.s1.r.d: Even if blank sections plenty, e fair if both people get same section number.
y-m-18-06.s.s1.explain: For fairness, Haeun and Doyun must get same number of sections. Number of blank sections no matter. With Haeun 6 and Doyun 3 sections, Haeun chance to get point (1/2) twice Doyun own (1/4), and with 5 and 4 sections, chances differ as 5/12 and 4/12.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.prompt: You dey make new spinner with 12 sections. Make 2 different fair spinners (Haeun sections h and Doyun sections d equal) where chance of ‘blank’ dey from 1/6 to 1/2. (Blank section number na k. h, d, k natural numbers and total na 12 sections.)
y-m-18-06.s.s2.hint.0: First think how to split Haeun and Doyun sections to make am fair.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write how many of 12 sections give blank chance of 1/6 and 1/2, then set di range.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.hint.2: Choose Haeun section number, work out wetin happen to remaining sections, and check say e meet conditions.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All section numbers na natural numbers of 1 or more.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c1: All three section numbers must be natural numbers of 1 or more.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Section numbers no add up to 12.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.ok.c3: Haeun and Doyun section numbers equal, so e fair.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c3: Haeun and Doyun section numbers different, so e no fair.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.ok.c4: Chance of blank dey between 1/6 and 1/2.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.fail.c4: Chance of blank no dey between 1/6 and 1/2.
y-m-18-06.s.s2.explain: (5, 5, 2), (4, 4, 4), and (3, 3, 6) fit work. If Haeun and Doyun section numbers equal, di rest na blank, so blank number na 12 minus 2h, an even number. Condition only work when k na 2, 4, or 6.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.prompt: Spinner (Haeun 3 sections, Doyun 3 sections, blank 6 sections) and spinner (Haeun 5 sections, Doyun 5 sections, blank 2 sections) both fair. Write wetin go different when you play with both spinners.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.hint.0: Compare how many of 12 sections mean nobody get point for both spinners.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write Haeun chance of getting point on each spinner.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You write how point frequency for one round different when many blanks dey and when few dey?
y-m-18-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You talk di difference while still noting say both spinners fair?
y-m-18-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You state chance with number, like how many of 12 sections?
y-m-18-06.s.s3.model.0: Both fair because Haeun and Doyun get same chance to win. But (5, 5, 2) get only 2 blank sections, so almost every time one of dem get point, while (3, 3, 6) get half blank, so plenty rounds nobody get point.
y-m-18-06.s.s3.model.1: Di more blank sections, di more likely one round go produce no points. Spinner with 3 sections each get 6/12 blank, so half di time nobody win, but e still fair.

y-m-18-01.title: Two groups with same average: their results similar too?
y-m-18-01.goal: Show with number examples you make yourself say individual results fit differ well well even when average same, and talk wetin you no fit know from average alone.
y-m-18-01.material:
For 6th-grade PE class, two groups (5 students each) do sit-ups for 1 minute. Their results na natural numbers from 0 and above (times).
Group A results: 8 times, 9 times, 10 times, 11 times, 12 times.
For Group B, na only this dem know: average of 5 students results na 10 times. Teacher talk, “Both groups get same average of 10 times, so dem be equally good groups.”
y-m-18-01.thinking.0: Separating wetin one average fit tell and wetin e no fit tell
y-m-18-01.thinking.1: Making data wey meet conditions by yourself (counterexample)
y-m-18-01.thinking.2: Talking wetin else need checking apart from average
y-m-18-01.prereq.0: Knowing meaning of average (value wey balance di data, 5th-grade level)
y-m-18-01.s.s1.prompt: For Group B, dem only know say average na 10 times. Choose all statements about B wey must be true.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write two or three sets of results for 5 students wey average na 10 times by yourself.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each statement, test one by one whether you fit make result set wey no match am.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.a: Total results for di 5 students na 50 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.a: This use relation say total results depend on average and number of people.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.b: All 5 students do at least 8, nobody do less.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.b: Even with average of 10 times, one student fit get very low result like 2. You may think average show ‘how every student perform.’
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.c: If one student do fewer than 10 times, another student must do more.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.c: You see say average na balance point where below-10 times and above-10 times balance each other.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.o.d: Among di 5 students, at least one do exactly 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.r.d: Average fit be value nobody actually get. Even if total na 50, like 8, 9, 11, 11, 11 times, nobody may get 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s1.explain: Total results for 5 students with average 10 must be 50 times, and if one student do less than 10, another must do more than 10 to make up. But you no fit say all did at least 8 or somebody surely did 10.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different sets of results for Group B with average 10 times, where difference between highest and lowest results na 12 times or more. (Results for 5 students a, b, c, d, e. Ones wey only change student order count as same result.)
y-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write wetin you fit know about all 5 students results from fact say average na 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one student wey do very few and think who fit make up the shortage.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.2: Subtract smallest result from biggest for your examples and check say difference na 12 or more.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Results na counts, so dem must be natural numbers.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.fail.c3: Average of 5 students no be 10 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.ok.c4: Highest and lowest results differ by 12 times or more.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.fail.c4: Difference between student wey do most and student wey do least less than 12 times.
y-m-18-01.s.s2.explain: e.g. 2, 4, 10, 16, and 18 times get average of 10 times, but highest and lowest results differ by 16 times. Even with same average, group wey results close together (A) and group wey results spread out no look same.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.prompt: Wetin you think about teacher statement, “Average same, so both groups equally good”? Write by comparing your examples above or Group A, and also say one thing wey you wan know apart from average.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.hint.0: Copy one line of results wey you made above as e be and put am beside A.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.hint.1: Start with sentence wey fill blank: ‘Average same, but ___ different.’
y-m-18-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: For di number example you give, e clear how results look different even though average same?
y-m-18-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You specifically write wetin you wan check apart from average (lowest, highest, difference between results, etc.)?
y-m-18-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You give reason instead of only writing ‘different’?
y-m-18-01.s.s3.model.0: Hard to agree. A results dey between 8 and 12 times, but di 2, 4, 10, 16, and 18 times wey I make get big range from 2 to 18. Even with same average, how spread out results be dey different, so I wan know highest and lowest too.
y-m-18-01.s.s3.model.1: Average alone say dem same, but for B wey I make, one student get only 2 and one get 18, so difference in ability big. Hard to say everybody do equally well. I wan see each student result.

y-m-18-02.title: When you toss two coins, which result come up more often?
y-m-18-02.topic: Chance: work am out by separating cases
y-m-18-02.goal: Compare two explanations (all 3 results same / look at coins separately and split cases) with experiment data, change your judgment, and explain why we split cases.
y-m-18-02.material:
You toss red coin and blue coin together. Each coin get same chance of heads and tails, and one coin no affect di other.
Jia: “There are 3 results: [both heads], [one head and one tail], and [both tails], so dem all get same chance.”
Minho: “There are two coins, so we must look at each coin result separately.”
y-m-18-02.thinking.0: Comparing two explanation models with data
y-m-18-02.thinking.1: Changing judgment and confidence after seeing data
y-m-18-02.thinking.2: Explaining why we count cases separately
y-m-18-02.prereq.0: Describing chance as ‘same / higher / lower’ (3rd–5th grade level)
y-m-18-02.s.s1.prompt: When people toss two coins, which one you think go happen most often? Choose wetin you think now.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write wetin blue coin fit show when red coin na heads.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write am same way when red coin na tails, then count total number of ways.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.a: Think whether reason dey make ‘both heads’ happen especially often. Each coin get same chance of heads.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.o.b: All three results dey happen about same number of times
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.b: Na explanation say three kinds of results get same chance. E never check whether each result fit happen same number of ways.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.c: You dey check whether more ways fit make that result. Next step fit test di evidence.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.o.d: You no fit talk anything before tossing
y-m-18-02.s.s1.r.d: Tossing dem na good way too, but you fit also work am out before by using fact say two coins dey.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.explain: For this step, na first guess. Many people also guess say ‘all three results same,’ but next steps go test am with data and case counting.
y-m-18-02.s.s1.acc.0: Na natural first guess. But we need test whether di ‘three results’ get same chance, so make we check data next.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.prompt: Dis na record of tossing two coins 40 times: both heads 9 times, one head and one tail 21 times, both tails 10 times. From dis record, how you judge Jia explanation?
y-m-18-02.s.s2.hint.0: If Jia explanation correct, estimate how many times each of three results suppose happen by dividing 40.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put estimate beside real results 9, 21, and 10, and compare how much each one different.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.a: Explanation say all three results same correct; 21 times just happen plenty by chance.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.a: You dey blame di data on chance. If three results same, each suppose happen about 13 times out of 40; how common e be to get 21?
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.b: Coins no fair, so one head and one tail happen plenty.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.b: Conditions say each coin get same chance of heads and tails. Before blaming coins, first check how dem count results.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.c: 40 small, so no judgment fit come from dis record.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.c: True say number of tosses small, but difference between 21 and 9 big well. Even if you no sure, you fit compare whether explanation match data.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.o.d: ‘One of each’ happen about twice as often as others, so Jia explanation doubtful.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.r.d: You compare whether explanation fit data by checking ratio of counts (9:21:10). 40 tosses no plenty, so ‘doubtful’ na good wording.
y-m-18-02.s.s2.explain: If all three results same, as Jia explain, each suppose happen about 13 times out of 40, but ‘one of each’ happen 21 times, about twice as many as others. 40 tosses no plenty so we no fit sure, but Jia explanation no match data well.
y-m-18-02.s.s3.prompt: Now explain am so Jia go understand. List possible results by telling the two coins apart, and say why ‘one head and one tail’ happen more often than ‘both heads.’
y-m-18-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write am like table, split into when red coin heads and when e tails.
y-m-18-02.s.s3.hint.1: Among cases wey you write, mark the ones wey count as ‘one of each.’
y-m-18-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we tell red coin and blue coin apart ...
y-m-18-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You write all possible cases without missing any, while telling red and blue coins apart?
y-m-18-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You clearly write how many cases make ‘one head and one tail’?
y-m-18-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You point out where Jia idea ‘3 outcomes, so dem same’ fail?
y-m-18-02.s.s3.model.0: If we tell red and blue coins apart, 4 cases dey: (heads, heads), (heads, tails), (tails, heads), (tails, tails). ‘One of each’ na two cases, (heads, tails) and (tails, heads), so e happen twice as often as ‘both heads.’
y-m-18-02.s.s3.model.1: Di two coins different, so (red heads, blue tails) and (red tails, blue heads) na different cases. Two of di 4 cases be one of each, so chance na 1/2, while both heads na 1/4.

y-m-18-04.title: If one bar twice as tall, sales too twice as plenty?
y-m-18-04.topic: Scale and comparison in bar graph
y-m-18-04.goal: Know say for bar graph wey scale no start at 0, ratio of bar heights and ratio of values fit different, and suggest ways to stop misunderstanding.
y-m-18-04.material: Number of books wey neighborhood bookstores A and B sell this month show for bar graph. Vertical scale start at bottom with 80 books, then 85, 90, 95, 100 books going up (e no start from 0 books). Measure bar height from bottom mark (80 books) reach end of bar. A bar end at 90 books and B bar end at 100 books. So B bar look about twice as tall as A bar.
y-m-18-04.thinking.0: Separating impression graph give from real values
y-m-18-04.thinking.1: Checking how scale starting point affect comparison
y-m-18-04.thinking.2: Making value pairs wey meet conditions and suggesting improvement
y-m-18-04.prereq.1: Comparing two numbers by multiplication (how many times)
y-m-18-04.s.s1.prompt: Three friends look this graph and talk. Choose all correct statements.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check directly with sales numbers wey scale show whether Jisu statement correct.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.hint.1: Look how many books vertical scale start from, and where people measure bar height from.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.a: Jisu: “B bar twice as tall, so sales exactly twice as much.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.a: You read bar height as the sales. Check scale to see where dem measure bar height from.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.b: Doyun: “If you read di scale, A na 90 books and B na 100 books. E no be twice.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.b: You check by reading values from scale instead of graph impression.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.c: Raon: “Scale start at 80 books, so ratio of bar heights and ratio of sales different.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.c: You point out say scale starting point affect comparison.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.o.d: Seoeun: “Graph itself wrong, so we no fit use data; we must do survey again.”
y-m-18-04.s.s1.r.d: Values for graph no wrong. How you read am fit make misunderstanding, but data no wrong.
y-m-18-04.s.s1.explain: Bar heights measure from 80 books, so A drawn 10 books high and B drawn 20 books high, making B look twice. But real sales, 90 and 100 books, no be twice. Graph itself no wrong; scale starting point make am easy to misunderstand.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.prompt: For graph like this, wey scale start from 80 books, make 2 different pairs of sales where B bar drawn exactly twice as tall as A but B real sales no pass 1.2 times A. (A and B na natural book numbers above 80.)
y-m-18-04.s.s2.hint.0: Use fact say bar height measure how much above 80 books.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.hint.1: Choose A, then work out how many books B need so B bar height go twice A.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.hint.2: With values wey you choose, check by yourself how many times B sales be compared with A.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.ok.c1: A more than 80 books, and both numbers natural numbers.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.fail.c1: A must pass 80 and both must be natural numbers.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.ok.c2: B bar height, measured from 80 books mark, na twice A bar height.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.fail.c2: B bar height, measured from 80 books mark, no be twice A bar height.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.ok.c3: B sales na 1.2 times A sales or less.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.fail.c3: B sales more than 1.2 times A sales.
y-m-18-04.s.s2.explain: For example, if (A, B)=(85, 90), bar heights na 5 and 10 books, exactly twice, but real sales about 1.06 times. For (90, 100), e about 1.11 times. If scale no start from 0, small difference fit look big.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.prompt: If you print this graph for bookstore newsletter, how you fit change or add something so readers no go misunderstand say ‘B sell twice as much’? Suggest at least one way.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.hint.0: Think whether Doyun or Raon method above go help reader.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think where person wey first see graph fit look to find values.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we ... di ... of graph, then ...
y-m-18-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Your method really reduce problem say graph ‘look like twice’?
y-m-18-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You help readers find values directly?
y-m-18-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Compared with other methods, you fit name one good thing about your suggestion?
y-m-18-04.s.s3.model.0: E go help to draw vertical scale from 0 books so bar heights match real size of sales.
y-m-18-04.s.s3.model.1: If you write values like 90 and 100 books above bars and mark say scale start at 80, readers go misunderstand less.

y-m-18-07.title: If we ask for soccer field, na wetin whole school think?
y-m-18-07.topic: Ways to collect data and representativeness
y-m-18-07.goal: Know say results fit change depending on how you choose people to survey, and design survey method by yourself wey represent whole school better.
y-m-18-07.material: Minseo, a 6th grader, wan find activity all 240 school students most want to do during break. Minseo ask 30 students wey gather for soccer field during break, and 24 (80%) answer ‘soccer.’ Minseo plan to announce, “80% of students for our school most want play soccer!”
y-m-18-07.thinking.0: Criticizing survey method wey result depend on
y-m-18-07.thinking.1: Changing your confidence after seeing new data
y-m-18-07.prereq.1: Arranging survey result in table (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-18-07.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you think about Minseo announcement?
y-m-18-07.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine what kind students gather for soccer field.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think how result fit change if same question ask for library or classroom.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.a: She only ask people for soccer field, so hard to say na whole school thinking.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.a: You point out say how person choose people to survey fit affect result.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.b: 30 students plenty enough, so dem fit announce am as e be.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.b: You judge by people number alone. Also look where and who she ask.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.c: 30 students too few, so no survey fit trusted.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.c: Number matter too, but who you ask come first. Even small group fit give clue if you choose am evenly.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.o.d: E reach 80%, so okay to say ‘most.’
y-m-18-07.s.s1.r.d: You judge only by high percentage. Look what kind people give that percentage.
y-m-18-07.s.s1.explain: More students wey like soccer fit gather for soccer field. So this result fit tell wetin ‘students wey gather for soccer field’ think, but hard to call am whole school opinion.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.prompt: Minseo change method and randomly choose 36 students by attendance number from list of all students, mixing grades and classes evenly. She ask dem, and 9 (25%) answer ‘soccer.’ Wetin you think now?
y-m-18-07.s.s2.hint.0: Compare who dem ask for both surveys.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine whether exactly 9 out of 36 go answer ‘soccer’ if dem draw another 36.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.a: 80% from first 30 students correct, but 25% from this 36 students wrong.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.a: You say one result surely correct and throw away di other. Look how two survey methods differ.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.b: Announce 52.5%, exact middle of both results, as whole school percentage.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.b: You just mix two sets of data collected with different methods. Since way to choose people different, mixing dem fit no get meaning.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.c: Result from 36 students closer to whole school, but exact value no known.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.c: You decide how much to trust am based on survey method, and also notice say 36 students no be whole school either.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.o.d: 36 more than 30, so announce 25% for whole school.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.r.d: You claim say results exactly same based only on people number. Different people fit give slightly different result.
y-m-18-07.s.s2.explain: 25% from 36 students chosen evenly more likely represent whole school than 80% from soccer-field survey. But 36 students no be whole school, so if another 36 chosen, result fit change small, and you no fit claim say exactly 25%.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.prompt: Design one survey method wey go show whole school thinking better. Write who you go ask and how you go choose dem.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.hint.0: Think whether all 240 students get chance to be chosen.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think how to divide dem so students no gather only in one grade or one place.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Na method wey give everybody equal (similar) chance to be chosen?
y-m-18-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You fit say how your method different from Minseo first method?
y-m-18-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You think about survey number or its range too?
y-m-18-07.s.s3.model.0: From each class I go randomly choose 3 students by attendance number and ask dem, so all classes get fair representation. If I ask inside classroom before class instead of break time, I no go meet only students wey gather for field.
y-m-18-07.s.s3.model.1: I go make one list for each grade and randomly choose same 20 students from each grade to ask. I want include opinion from every grade.

y-m-18-08.title: How many cm sunflower go reach for week 8?
y-m-18-08.topic: Line graphs and predicting wetin go happen next
y-m-18-08.goal: Predict next event from pattern of change for graph, know say prediction get assumptions, and adjust prediction and confidence when new data show.
y-m-18-08.material: Dem measure sunflower height for classroom pot same day every week and show am for line graph. Height dey cm, and take every value as exact measurement. Dem show data one week at a time.
y-m-18-08.thinking.0: Predicting from pattern of change in data
y-m-18-08.thinking.2: Adjusting prediction after seeing new data and information
y-m-18-08.s.s1.prompt: Each time data show, choose how you go predict height for week 8.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write how many cm height change from previous week each time.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write one sentence explaining wetin your prediction assume go continue.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.info: Week 1 na 5 cm, week 2 na 8 cm, week 3 na 11 cm, and week 4 na 14 cm. Graph points nearly form one straight line.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: How you go predict height for week 8?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.after: E grow 3 cm every week for 4 weeks, so if same speed continue, week 8 na 5+3×7=26 cm. But assumption say ‘same speed go continue’ matter.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: E go continue grow 3 cm every week reach about 26 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You continue pattern wey happen so far into future. Better if you remember say prediction assume pattern go continue.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: E no go grow again and go remain about 14 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Data never give clue yet say height don stop growing.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: About 26 cm, but we must check whether same speed continue
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You think about condition for prediction together with prediction.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 4 weeks data too little to make any prediction
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: No be say no clue at all. Steady growth for 4 weeks na information too.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.info: Week 5 na 17 cm, week 6 na 19 cm, and week 7 na 20 cm. Growth amount dey reduce: 3 cm, 2 cm, 1 cm.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now how you go predict height for week 8?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.after: Growth amount reduce like 3, 2, 1 cm, so week 8 likely near 20 cm. First assumption ‘3 cm every week’ no fit new data again.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Following first pattern, e go still be about 26 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You dey hold on to first pattern. What if you include new data from weeks 5 to 7?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: E go be value wey near 20 cm
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You adjust prediction to show change during last 3 weeks.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Data no show evidence say height dey shrink.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Treat am as near 20 cm and measure week 8 to check
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You mention recent changes and say we must keep checking.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.info: Seed packet talk, ‘This variety grow to full height about 20 cm.’ Dem measure 20 cm for week 8, 20 cm for week 9, 20 cm for week 10.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: How you now judge first prediction of 26 cm using first 4 weeks data?
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.after: Pattern from first 4 weeks fit up to that point. But height no continue growing at same speed, and new information about variety maximum height change assumption. When predicting what come next, write assumption and adjust when new data arrive.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Method to predict next thing from graph useless altogether
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Wrong prediction no mean method useless. Check which assumption fail.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: At first e sound reasonable, but assumption say same growth speed fail.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You point out assumption behind prediction and how new information change am.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: First prediction correct; later measurement strange
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You try hold on to first prediction while ignoring later data and seed-packet information.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Points for first 4 weeks no dey on one line
y-m-18-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: First data show steady growth. Problem no be data, na assumption about future change.
y-m-18-08.s.s1.reflect: Was e reasonable for person wey only get first 4 weeks data to predict about 26 cm for week 8? Wetin you fit add so e no too bad if prediction later turn wrong?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.prompt: Friend wey only get first 4 weeks data ask, “How many cm e go reach for week 8?” Give prediction with conditions.
y-m-18-08.s.s2.hint.0: First write how many cm e grow each week for 4 weeks, then continue and see how many cm e go reach which week if same thing continue.
y-m-18-08.s.s2.hint.1: Add one sentence wey end with ‘if ___.’
y-m-18-08.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If e continue ... like now, then ...
y-m-18-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You write predicted value and pattern wey e follow (e.g. 3 cm each week)?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You write at least one thing wey fit make prediction wrong if e change?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You suggest wetin to check in future?
y-m-18-08.s.s2.model.0: If e continue growing 3 cm every week like now, e go reach about 26 cm by week 8. But nothing guarantee say e go keep same speed.
y-m-18-08.s.s2.model.1: E grow steadily up to week 4, so I predict about 26 cm. But if growth speed change, prediction fit wrong, so make we measure every week and adjust am.
